parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain how a uniform magnetic field and a uniform electric field may be used as a velocity selector for charged particles.

markscheme_points.text: electric and magnetic fields at right-angles
no deviation for particles with selected vel

hints: Hint 1: Think about how you could arrange the two fields so that a moving charged particle feels a push from the electric field and a push from the magnetic field in opposite directions.
Hint 2: Consider how each push depends on speed - one push is the same for all speeds, while the other push grows larger when the particle moves faster.
Hint 3: Think about what happens when those two opposite pushes are exactly equal in size, so the particle goes straight through, and what this tells you about its speed.
parts.proper_answer: E and B fields are uniform and perpendicular to each other and to the particle velocity. Electric force $qE$ and magnetic force $Bqv$ act in opposite directions. Only particles with $qE = Bqv$, i.e. $v = E/B$, have zero resultant force and pass through undeflected.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set the fields crossed**
Imagine sitting beside the particle as it flies in. You need the electric push to try to deflect it one way and the magnetic push to try to deflect it back the other way. That only works if the $E$ field and the $B$ field are at right angles to each other, and both are at right angles to the velocity of the particle.

Step 2: **Write the two opposing forces**
The electric field always pushes with $$F_E = qE$$ independent of speed. The magnetic field pushes sideways on a moving charge with $$F_B = Bqv$$ when velocity is normal to the field. By arranging the field directions correctly these two forces point in opposite directions.

Step 3: **Pick out the selected velocity**
Most particles feel a larger push one way or the other and are deflected into a stop. Only one speed gives perfect balance: $$qE = Bqv$$ $$v = E/B$$ Those particles feel zero resultant force and continue straight through the selector. That is how the crossed fields select velocity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Particles having mass $m$ and charge $+1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ pass through a velocity selector. They then enter a region of uniform magnetic field of magnetic flux density $94\text{ mT}$ with speed $3.4 \times 10^{4}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, as shown in Fig. 8.1.

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

The direction of the uniform magnetic field is into the page and normal to the direction in which the particles are moving.

The particles are moving in a vacuum in a circular arc of diameter $15.0\text{ cm}$.

Show that the mass of one of the particles is $20\text{ u}$.

markscheme_points.text: magnetic force equals/is the centripetal fo

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 8.1 - the particle enters normal to a uniform $B$ field into the page and curves into a circular arc, so think about what provides the inward force for circular motion.
Hint 2: Recall that steady circular motion needs a centripetal force $mv^2/r$ towards the centre, and here it is the magnetic force that supplies it.
Hint 3: Be careful with units and geometry - convert $94\text{ mT}$ to tesla and use the radius, which is half the $15.0\text{ cm}$ diameter, in metres.
Hint 4: Once you calculate the mass in kg, divide by $1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ to express the answer in u and confirm it is about 20.
parts.proper_answer: $Bqv = mv^2/r$ gives $m = Bqr/v$. With $r = 0.0750\text{ m}$, $m = (94 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.0750)/(3.4 \times 10^{4}) = 3.32 \times 10^{-26}\text{ kg} = 3.32 \times 10^{-26} / 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \approx 20\text{ u}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why the path is circular**
The particle enters at right angles to a uniform $B$ field. The magnetic force $Bqv$ is always perpendicular to velocity, so it acts as a sideways steering force. That is exactly what is needed for uniform circular motion, so the magnetic force is the centripetal force.

Step 2: **Equate magnetic force to centripetal force**
For a particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moving at speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$: $$Bqv = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$ Cancelling one $v$ and rearranging for mass: $$m = \frac{Bqr}{v}$$ This is the mass spectrometer equation.

Step 3: **Insert the numbers carefully**
From the question $B = 94\text{ mT} = 94 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$, $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $v = 3.4 \times 10^{4}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The diameter is $15.0\text{ cm}$, so $$r = \frac{0.150}{2} = 0.0750\text{ m}$$ Then $$m = \frac{(94 \times 10^{-3})(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.0750)}{3.4 \times 10^{4}} \approx 3.32 \times 10^{-26}\text{ kg}$$

Step 4: **Convert kg to u**
One unified atomic mass unit $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. So $$m \text{ in u} = \frac{3.32 \times 10^{-26}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 20$$ Hence the mass is $20\text{ u}$, as required.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: On Fig. 8.1, sketch the path in the uniform magnetic field of a particle of mass $22\text{ u}$ having the same charge and speed as the particle in (b).
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the radius $r = mv/Bq$ changes when only the mass increases from 20 u to 22 u, with the same charge, speed and $B$ field.
Hint 2: Picture starting from the same entry slit - if the particle turns less tightly, what shape will the path have and where will it hit the detector plate compared with the 15.0 cm mark?
parts.proper_answer: Same entry point, semicircular path in same rotational sense as in Fig. 8.1 but with larger radius, so diameter > 15.0 cm.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the radius rule**
From $Bqv = mv^2/r$ you get $$r = \frac{mv}{Bq}$$ With $v$, $B$ and $q$ unchanged, radius is directly proportional to mass. A $22\text{ u}$ particle is heavier than a $20\text{ u}$ particle, so it has more inertia and bends less tightly.

Step 2: **Sketch the new path**
Start at the same entry slit and draw a semicircle curving in the same direction as the dashed path in Fig. 8.1. Make the radius clearly larger, so it lands on the top plate beyond the $15.0\text{ cm}$ position. That larger diameter shows the heavier isotope is separated.
